Why is Gaza drowning? Images of floods engulfing Gaza have gone viral. Most coverage focuses on the humanitarian catastrophe. Few explain what caused it. Since October 2023, Israeli forces have destroyed nearly all of Gaza’s infrastructure. Up to 68 million tons of rubble now blanket the Strip. Homes, schools, hospitals, and basic services have been flattened, with at least 90 percent of the territory destroyed. Now, as winter sets in, the first rains are making what is left unlivable. At least five people have been killed after sand embankments collapsed in the downpour. None of this is new. The Israeli plan to make Gaza unlivable has been unfolding for years. In 2012, the UN warned that Gaza could be unlivable by 2020 because of repeated Israeli assaults, a crippling blockade, the collapse of its aquifer, energy shortages, and mass unemployment. Despite the so-called ceasefire, our reporter in Gaza describes a situation that is impossible to endure: no shelter, no aid, and a ban on rebuilding. Conditions are getting worse by the day.” @specter_affairs

This year’s olive harvest has been the most violent in recent memory, with settler attacks on Palestinian farmers reaching a new high. But for Masafer Yatta, this is only the latest escalation in a decades-long campaign by the Israeli state to expel Palestinians from their land by any means necessary. Working in coordination with the army and police, nearby settlers wage a ceaseless battle against the Palestinians living in this area. Professor Ilan Pappé describes what has been happening to Masafer Yatta since the 1970’s as “incremental colonization, ethnic cleansing, and oppression,” and to be here is to see it firsthand. But the people of Masafer Yatta have earned a reputation for themselves for their resistance to state and settler terror. They simply refuse to leave, and the Israelis simply won’t stop trying to force them to. The Nakba never ended. We’re just watching its latest act.

Palestine is not just a place on a map. Palestine is its people, its history, its culture, its language, its traditions, its children, its mothers, its fathers, and generations of people who deserve to live in peace, freedom, and dignity. You can destroy buildings, but you cannot destroy a people’s identity. You can silence voices, but you cannot erase their stories. You can take away homes, but you cannot take away the memories, the roots, and the love people carry in their hearts. The people of Palestine deserve what every human being deserves: the right to live, the right to feel safe, the right to dream, the right to grow up without fear, and the right to have a future. Behind every headline, every photograph, and every statistic are real human beings. Families. Children. People with dreams, hopes, names, and stories. Their lives matter. Their voices matter. Their suffering must never become something the world simply scrolls past. Supporting Palestine means standing for humanity, justice, freedom, and human dignity. It means refusing to look away. It means remembering those whose voices are not always heard and making sure their stories are not forgotten. To every Palestinian who continues to hold on to their identity, culture, heritage, and hope: the world sees you, the world hears you, and your existence matters. Palestine is not forgotten. Palestine is not invisible. Palestine is not alone. May the children of Palestine know a future filled with peace instead of fear. May families be reunited. May people return to their homes. May justice prevail, and may every human being live with the dignity they deserve. From the river to the sea, may all people live in freedom, safety, and dignity. We will remember. We will speak. We will stand for humanity. FREE PALESTINE 🇵🇸🤍 #palestine #recommendations #fypシ

Children in Gaza are being forced to trade their childhoods for survival as poverty, displacement and devastation from Israel’s war push families to the brink. Instead of attending school, many Palestinian children are selling food and water, collecting scrap metal, scavenging for firewood and working long hours to help feed their families. Some have become their households’ sole breadwinners after losing parents or other relatives. According to UNICEF, economic desperation has forced one in four families to resort to hazardous or exploitative child labor, with children as young as six taking on dangerous work. The crisis is deepening concerns about an entire generation growing up without education, stability or safety. Israel’s military offensive has devastated Gaza’s economy, destroyed schools and displaced hundreds of thousands of families, leaving children exposed to exploitation, malnutrition and severe psychological trauma. UNICEF estimates that around 60,000 children have lost one or both parents during the war and its aftermath. Aid organizations warn that without sustained humanitarian assistance, access to education and opportunities for families to earn a living, thousands more children could be pushed into work simply to survive.
